Kinetic layers and coupling conditions for macroscopic equations on networks I: the wave equation

R. Borsche11 1 Technische Universität Kaiserslautern, Department of Mathematics, Erwin-Schrödinger-Straße, 67663 Kaiserslautern, Germany ({borsche, klar}@mathematik.uni-kl.de)    A. Klar11footnotemark: 1 22 2 Fraunhofer ITWM, Fraunhoferplatz 1, 67663 Kaiserslautern, Germany
Abstract

We consider kinetic and associated macroscopic equations on networks. The general approach will be explained in this paper for a linear kinetic BGK model and the corresponding limit for small Knudsen number, which is the wave equation. Coupling conditions for the macroscopic equations are derived from the kinetic conditions via an asymptotic analysis near the nodes of the network. This analysis leads to the consideration of a fixpoint problem involving the coupled solutions of kinetic half-space problems. A new approximate method for the solution of kinetic half-space problems is derived and used for the determination of the coupling conditions. Numerical comparisons between the solutions of the macroscopic equation with different coupling conditions and the kinetic solution are presented for the case of tripod and more complicated networks.

Keywords. Kinetic layer, coupling condition, kinetic half-space problem, networks

AMS Classification. 82B40, 90B10,65M08

1 Introduction

There have been many attempts to define coupling conditions for macroscopic partial differential equations on networks including, for example, drift-diffusion equations, scalar hyperbolic equations, or hyperbolic systems like the wave equation or Euler type models, see for example [7, 10, 9, 3, 2, 15, 1, 20, 41, 6, 29, 14]. In [14, 29] coupling conditions for scalar hyperbolic equations on networks are discussed and investigated. [1, 20, 41] treat the wave equation and general nonlinear hyperbolic systems are considered in [9, 3, 2, 15, 6]. We finally note, that, for example, for hyperbolic systems on networks there are still many unsolved problems, like finding suitable coupling conditions without restricting to subsonic situations.

On the other hand, coupling conditions for kinetic equations on networks have been discussed in a much smaller number of publications, see [21, 30, 8]. In [8] a first attempt to derive a coupling condition for a macroscopic equation from the underlying kinetic model has been presented for the case of a kinetic equations for chemotaxis. In the present paper, we will present a more general and more accurate procedure. It is motivated by the classical procedure to find kinetic slip boundary conditions for macroscopic equations based on the analysis of the kinetic layer [4, 5, 23, 24, 40]. In this work, we will derive coupling conditions for macroscopic equations on a network from underlying microscopic or kinetic models via an asymptotic analysis of the situation near the nodes. To explain the basic approach we concentrate on a simple linear BGK-type kinetic model with the linear wave equation as the associated macroscopic model. More complicated problems and, in particular, nonlinear models will be discussed in future work.

The paper is organized in the following way. In section 2 we discuss the kinetic and macroscopic equations and the boundary and coupling conditions for these equations. In section 3 kinetic boundary layers are discussed, as well as an asymptotic analysis of the kinetic equations near the nodes. This leads to an abstract formulation of the coupling conditions for the macroscopic equations at the nodes based on a fix-point problem involving kinetic half-space equations. In the following section 4 an approximate coupling condition is derived based on the so called Maxwell approximation of the half-space problem. A refined method to determine the solution of the half space problems is derived, compared to previous approximate solution methods for half-space problems and applied to the problem of finding accurate coupling conditions for the macroscopic equations in sections 5. Moreover, the macroscopic equations on the network with the different coupling conditions are numerically compared to each other and to the full solutions of the kinetic equations on the network in section 6. The results show the very good approximation of the underlying kinetic model by the macroscopic model with the new coupling conditions.

2 Equations and boundary and coupling conditions

We consider the linear kinetic BGK model in 1D for x∈ℝ,v∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R},v\in\mathbb{R}.

∂tf+v​∂xf=−1ϵ​(f−(ρ+va2​q)​M​(v))\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \partial_{t}f+v\partial_{x}f=-\frac{1}{\epsilon}\left(f-\left(\rho+\frac{v}{a^{2}}q\right)M(v)\right)\end{aligned} (1)

The associated macroscopic equation for ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0 is the wave equation

∂tρ+∂xq=0∂tq+∂x(a2​ρ)=0.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \partial_{t}\rho+\partial_{x}q=0\\ \partial_{t}q+\partial_{x}(a^{2}\rho)=0\ .\end{aligned} (2)

∂tf+v​∂xf=−1ϵ​(f−(ρϵ+va2​qϵ)​12)\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \partial_{t}f+v\partial_{x}f=-\frac{1}{\epsilon}\left(f-(\rho_{\epsilon}+\frac{v}{a^{2}}q_{\epsilon})\frac{1}{2}\right)\end{aligned} (3)

with a2=13a^{2}=\frac{1}{3} or

∂tf+v​∂xf=−1ϵ​(f−(ρϵ2+32​v​qϵ))\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \partial_{t}f+v\partial_{x}f=-\frac{1}{\epsilon}\left(f-(\frac{\rho_{\epsilon}}{2}+\frac{3}{2}vq_{\epsilon})\right)\end{aligned} (4)

with

ρϵ=∫−11f⁡(v)​𝑑v,qϵ=∫−11v​f​(v)​𝑑v.\rho_{\epsilon}=\int_{-1}^{1}f(v)dv,\quad q_{\epsilon}=\int_{-1}^{1}vf(v)dv\ .

The associated macroscopic equation is again (2) with a2=13a^{2}=\frac{1}{3}.

2.1 Boundary conditions

For x∈[0,b]x\in[0,b] we prescribe for the kinetic equation

f⁡(0,v),v>0,f⁡(b,v),v<0.f(0,v),v>0,\;f(b,v),v<0.

For (2) the boundary conditions are given in characteristic variables [39]. The corresponding Riemann Invariants are

r1/2=q∓a​ρ.\displaystyle r_{1/2}=q\mp a\rho. (5)

As boundary data the value of q+a​ρq+a\rho at the left boundary and q−a​ρq-a\rho at the right boundary are prescribed.

2.2 Coupling conditions

If these equations are considered on a network, it is sufficient to study a single coupling point. At each node so called coupling conditions are required. In the following we consider a node connecting nn edges, which are oriented away from the node, as in Figure 1. Each edge ii is parametrized by the interval [0,bi][0,b_{i}] and the kinetic and macroscopic quantities are denoted by fif^{i} and ρi,qi\rho^{i},q^{i} respectively. A possible choice of coupling conditions for the kinetic problem are given by

fi​(0,v)=∑j=1nci​j​fj​(0,−v),v>0,\displaystyle f^{i}(0,v)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{ij}f^{j}(0,-v),v>0, (6)

compare [8]. The total mass in the system is conserved, if

∑i=1nci​j=1\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{ij}=1 (7)

holds. In the following we use the vector notation

f+=C​f−,v>0,\displaystyle f^{+}=Cf^{-},v>0\ ,

where f+=(f1​(0,v),…,fn​(0,v))f^{+}=(f^{1}(0,v),\dots,f^{n}(0,v)) and f−=(f1​(0,−v),…,fn​(0,−v))f^{-}=(f^{1}(0,-v),\dots,f^{n}(0,-v)). The coupling conditions for the macroscopic quantities are conditions on the characteristic variables

r2i​(0)=qi​(0)+a​ρi​(0)\displaystyle r_{2}^{i}(0)=q^{i}(0)+a\rho^{i}(0)

using the given values of

r1i​(0)=qi​(0)−a​ρi​(0).\displaystyle r_{1}^{i}(0)=q^{i}(0)-a\rho^{i}(0)\ .

We refer to [15, 22] for systems of macroscopic equations on networks. In the following we will derive, via asymptotic analysis, macroscopic coupling conditions from the kinetic coupling conditions (6).

3 Boundary and coupling conditions for macroscopic equations via kinetic layer analysis

3.1 Boundary conditions

A kinetic layer analysis, see [4, 11, 17, 22], at the left boundary of the interval [0,b][0,b], i.e. a rescaling of the spatial variable in equation (1) with ϵ\epsilon, gives to first order in ϵ\epsilon the following stationary kinetic half space problem for x∈[0,∞]x\in[0,\infty]

v​∂xφ=−(φ−(ρ+va2​q)​M​(v)),\displaystyle\begin{aligned} v\partial_{x}\varphi=-\left(\varphi-\left(\rho+\frac{v}{a^{2}}q\right)M(v)\right)\ ,\end{aligned} (8)

where ρ\rho and qq are the zeroth and first moments of φ\varphi. At x=0x=0 the boundary conditions for the half space problem are

φ⁡(0,v)=k⁡(v)=f⁡(0,v),v>0.\varphi(0,v)=k(v)=f(0,v),v>0\ .

On the left side, i.e. at x=∞x=\infty, a condition is prescribing an arbitrary linear combination of the invariants of the half-space problem <v​φ><v\varphi> and <v2​φ><v^{2}\varphi> . Here, and in the following we use the notation <φ>=∫φ​𝑑v<\varphi>=\int\varphi dv and <φ>+=∫v>0φdv<\varphi>_{+}=\int_{v>0}\varphi dv or <φ>−=∫v<0φdv<\varphi>_{-}=\int_{v<0}\varphi dv. We use the values of the first Riemann Invariant (5) r1=q−a​ρr_{1}=q-a\rho of the macroscopic system (2) to fix

<(v−v2a)​φ>=r1.<\left(v-\frac{v^{2}}{a}\right)\varphi>=r_{1}.

The boundary condition for (2) is obtained by determining r2r_{2} from the asymptotic solution of the half space problem and setting r2=q∞+a​ρ∞r_{2}=q_{\infty}+a\rho_{\infty}. The values ρ∞\rho_{\infty} and q∞q_{\infty} are the macroscopic quantities associated to the solution of the half-space problem at infinity, which has the form

φ⁡(∞,v)=(ρ∞+va2​q∞)​M​(v).\varphi(\infty,v)=\left(\rho_{\infty}+\frac{v}{a^{2}}q_{\infty}\right)M(v)\ .

The solution of the half space problem is also used to determine the outgoing distribution

A⁡[k]​(v)=f⁡(0,v)=φ⁡(0,v),v<0,A[k](v)=f(0,v)=\varphi(0,v),v<0\ ,

where the notation AA is used for the so called Albedo operator of the half space problem. The structure of a half space problem is illustrated in Figure 2.

3.2 Coupling conditions

We use the corresponding procedure to determine the coupling conditions for the macroscopic equations.

Starting from the kinetic coupling conditions

fi​(0,v)=∑j=1nci​j​fj​(0,−v),v>0\displaystyle f^{i}(0,v)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{ij}f^{j}(0,-v),v>0

we determine the coupling conditions for the macroscopic equations in the following way. We use the kinetic coupling conditions to obtain conditions on the in- and outgoing solutions of the half space problems on the different arcs. That means

φi​(0,v)=∑j=1nci​j​φj​(0,−v),v>0\displaystyle\varphi^{i}(0,v)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{ij}\varphi^{j}(0,-v),v>0

or, if we denote the ingoing function of the half-space problem on arc ii by ki​(v),v>0k^{i}(v),v>0 and the outgoing solution by Ai​[ki]​(v),v<0A^{i}[k^{i}](v),v<0

ki​(v)=∑j=1nci​j​Aj​[kj]​(−v),v>0.\displaystyle k^{i}(v)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{ij}A^{j}[k^{j}](-v),v>0\ . (9)

This is a fix point equation for ki,i=1​…,nk^{i},i=1\ldots,n. Additional conditions are needed to solve the half-space problems, i.e.

<(v−v2a)​φi>=r1i<\left(v-\frac{v^{2}}{a}\right)\varphi^{i}>=r^{i}_{1}

with r1i=qi−a​ρir^{i}_{1}=q^{i}-a\rho^{i}. The coupling conditions for the wave equation are conditions on the outgoing characteristic variables at x=0x=0. We define

r2i​(0)=q∞i​[ki]+a​ρ∞i​[ki].\displaystyle r^{i}_{2}(0)=q^{i}_{\infty}[k^{i}]+a\rho^{i}_{\infty}[k^{i}].

The main task is now to find tractable expressions for these coupling conditions. In the next section we discuss the so called Maxwell method to solve the half-space problem approximately and the resulting approximate coupling conditions. In further sections a new refined method to determine the solution of the half space problems based on half moment equations is derived and applied to the problem of finding accurate coupling conditions. Finally, the results are compared to full solutions of the kinetic equations on the network and to other approximate solution methods for the half-space problem.

4 Approximate solution of the half space problem via half-fluxes and approximate coupling conditions

To solve kinetic half space problem approximately a variety of different methods can be found in the literature. Approaches via a Galerkin method can be found in [16, 32, 31]. Approximate methods to determine only the asymptotic states and outgoing distributions can be found in [25, 33, 34]. For the determination of the macroscopic boundary conditions we use in this section a simple approximation, the so called Maxwell approximation, see [36, 35].

4.1 Approximate solution of the half space problem

We use the equality of half-fluxes

<vk(v)>+=<v(ρ∞+va2q∞)M>+\displaystyle<vk(v)>_{+}=<v\left(\rho_{\infty}+\frac{v}{a^{2}}q_{\infty}\right)M>_{+}

to obtain one condition. Together with the first Riemann Invariant

q∞−a​ρ∞=q−a​ρ=r1​(0)=C=const.\displaystyle q_{\infty}-a\rho_{\infty}=q-a\rho=r_{1}(0)=C=\mbox{const.}

this determines ρ∞\rho_{\infty} and q∞q_{\infty}. This can be rewritten as

(a​12​π12−a1)​(ρ∞q∞)=(<vk>+C)\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}a\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}&\frac{1}{2}\\ -a&1\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\rho_{\infty}\\ q_{\infty}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}<vk>_{+}\\ C\end{array}\right)\

with the solution

(ρ∞q∞)=1a⁡(12​π−12)​(<vk>+−C2a<vk>++a​C2​π).\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\rho_{\infty}\\ q_{\infty}\end{array}\right)=\frac{1}{a\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}-\frac{1}{2}\right)}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}<vk>_{+}-\frac{C}{2}\\ a<vk>_{+}+\frac{aC}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\end{array}\right)\ .

The outgoing distribution is approximated by

φ⁡(0,v)=(ρ∞+va2​q∞)​M​(v),v<0.\varphi(0,v)=\left(\rho_{\infty}+\frac{v}{a^{2}}q_{\infty}\right)M(v),v<0.
Remark 1.

For bounded velocity space and equation (3) we have

(1412−a1)​(ρ∞q∞)=(<vk>+C).\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\frac{1}{4}&\frac{1}{2}\\ -a&1\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\rho_{\infty}\\ q_{\infty}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}<vk>_{+}\\ C\end{array}\right)\ .

4.2 Approximate coupling conditions

The fix-point problem (9) is in the present case approximated by the problem

ki​(v)=∑j=1nci​j​(ρ∞j​[kj]−va2​q∞j​[kj])​M​(−v),v>0.\displaystyle k^{i}(v)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{ij}\left(\rho_{\infty}^{j}[k^{j}]-\frac{v}{a^{2}}q_{\infty}^{j}[k^{j}]\right)M(-v),v>0.

Thus, the asymptotic values are determined by

(a​12​π12−a1)​(ρ∞iq∞i)=(∑jci​j​(ρ∞j​a2​π−q∞j2)r1i​(0)).\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}a\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}&\frac{1}{2}\\ -a&1\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\rho^{i}_{\infty}\\ q^{i}_{\infty}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\sum_{j}c_{ij}\left(\rho_{\infty}^{j}\frac{a}{\sqrt{2\pi}}-\frac{q_{\infty}^{j}}{2}\right)\\ r^{i}_{1}(0)\end{array}\right).

These values can be assigned to the states of the wave equation (2) at the coupling point by

r2i​(0)=q∞i+a​ρ∞i.r^{i}_{2}(0)=q^{i}_{\infty}+a\rho^{i}_{\infty}.\\

Summing the first equation of (4.2) for all i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n and using the conservation property of the kinetic coupling conditions (7) directly yields the conservation of mass in the macroscopic variables

∑i=1nq∞i=0.\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}q_{\infty}^{i}=0. (22)

In the special case of a uniform node, i.e. ci​j=1n−1c_{ij}=\frac{1}{n-1} for i≠ji\neq j and ci​j=0c_{ij}=0 for i=ji=j we have

a​12​π​ρ∞i+12​q∞i=1n−1​∑j≠i(a2​π​ρ∞j−q∞j2).\displaystyle a\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\rho^{i}_{\infty}+\frac{1}{2}q^{i}_{\infty}=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j\neq i}\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\rho^{j}_{\infty}-\frac{q^{j}_{\infty}}{2}\right).

Multiplying by 2​π\sqrt{2\pi} and adding 2​πn\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{n} times (22) we obtain

a​ρ∞i+2​π2​n−2n​q∞i=1n−1​∑j≠i(a​ρ∞j+2​π2​n−2n​q∞j)i=1,…,n.\displaystyle a\rho^{i}_{\infty}+\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{2}\frac{n-2}{n}q^{i}_{\infty}=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j\neq i}\left(a\rho^{j}_{\infty}+\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{2}\frac{n-2}{n}q^{j}_{\infty}\right)\qquad i=1,\dots,n.

These nn equations are not linearly independent and they can be reformulated as

a​ρ∞i+2​π2​n−2n​q∞i=a​ρ∞j+2​π2​n−2n​q∞ji,j=1,…,n,i≠j.\displaystyle a\rho^{i}_{\infty}+\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{2}\frac{n-2}{n}q^{i}_{\infty}=a\rho^{j}_{\infty}+\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{2}\frac{n-2}{n}q^{j}_{\infty}\qquad i,j=1,\dots,n\ ,i\neq j.

Thus we have found a macroscopic invariant at the coupling point, i.e.

ρ+2​π2​a​n−2n​q.\displaystyle\rho+\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{2a}\frac{n-2}{n}q. (23)
Remark 2.

For bounded velocity space we have

14​ρ∞i+12​q∞i=∑jci​j​(14​ρ∞j−q∞j2).\displaystyle\frac{1}{4}\rho^{i}_{\infty}+\frac{1}{2}q^{i}_{\infty}=\sum_{j}c_{ij}\left(\frac{1}{4}\rho^{j}_{\infty}-\frac{q^{j}_{\infty}}{2}\right).

For a uniform node this leads to

ρ∞i+2​(n−2)n​q∞i=ρ∞j+2​(n−2)n​q∞j\displaystyle\rho^{i}_{\infty}+\frac{2(n-2)}{n}q^{i}_{\infty}=\rho^{j}_{\infty}+\frac{2(n-2)}{n}q^{j}_{\infty}

and to the invariant

ρ∞+2​(n−2)n​q∞.\displaystyle\rho_{\infty}+\frac{2(n-2)}{n}q_{\infty}. (24)

For example for n=3n=3, we obtain for the above invariant (23) a factor 6​π6∼0.72360\frac{\sqrt{6\pi}}{6}\sim 0.72360 for a2=13a^{2}=\frac{1}{3} in contrast to the value 23\frac{2}{3} for the bounded velocity case. Thus although the kinetic coupling conditions and the macroscopic equations (2) are identical we obtain different coupling conditions for a model with bounded velocity, since the half space problems are different.

Remark 3.

Another direct approach to obtain coupling conditions for the wave equation has been used in [8]. Using a full moment approximation of the distribution function in the case of bounded velocities, i.e. using

f±​(v)=ρ2±32​v​q,v∈[0,1]f^{\pm}(v)=\frac{\rho}{2}\pm\frac{3}{2}vq,\quad v\in[0,1]

in the kinetic coupling conditions (6), one obtains after integration over the positive velocities

ρ∞i+32​q∞i=∑jci​j​(ρ∞j−32​q∞j).\displaystyle\rho^{i}_{\infty}+\frac{3}{2}q^{i}_{\infty}=\sum_{j}c_{ij}\left(\rho^{j}_{\infty}-\frac{3}{2}q^{j}_{\infty}\right)\ .

This leads, for a uniform node, to the invariant

ρ∞+3​(n−2)2​n​q∞.\displaystyle\rho_{\infty}+\frac{3(n-2)}{2n}q_{\infty}\ . (25)

In the case of unbounded velocities we obtain

ρ∞i+2a​π​q∞i=∑jci​j​(ρ∞j−2a​π​q∞j).\displaystyle\rho^{i}_{\infty}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{a\sqrt{\pi}}q^{i}_{\infty}=\sum_{j}c_{ij}\left(\rho^{j}_{\infty}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{a\sqrt{\pi}}q^{j}_{\infty}\right)\ .

and the invariant

ρ∞+2a​π​(n−2)n​q∞.\displaystyle\rho_{\infty}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{a\sqrt{\pi}}\frac{(n-2)}{n}q_{\infty}\ . (26)

5 Coupling conditions via approximation by half-moment equations

In this section we develop a refined method to solve the half-space problem based on a half moment approximation and use it for the derivation of refined coupling conditions. We begin with the case of equation (3). For further approaches to the approximate solution of half space problems we refer to [25, 33, 37].

5.1 The case of a bounded velocity domain

Consider the linear BGK model with bounded velocities (4) and the corresponding limit equation (2).

5.1.1 Half moment equations

We determine a half moment approximation for the half-space solution, compare [8]. We define

ρϵ−\displaystyle\rho_{\epsilon}^{-} =∫−10f(v)dv,\displaystyle=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{0}f(v)dv\ ,\qquad ρϵ+\displaystyle\rho_{\epsilon}^{+} =∫01f⁡(v)​dv,\displaystyle=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}f(v)dv\ , (27)
qϵ−\displaystyle q_{\epsilon}^{-} =∫−10v​f​(v)​dv,\displaystyle=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{0}vf(v)dv\ , qϵ+\displaystyle q_{\epsilon}^{+} =∫01v​f​(v)​dv.\displaystyle=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}vf(v)dv\ .

As closure assumption we use the following approximation of the distribution function ff by affine linear functions in vv to determine half-moment equations, see [8] and references therein.

f⁡(v)=a++v​b+,v≥0\displaystyle f(v)=a^{+}+vb^{+},\ v\geq 0 and f⁡(v)=a−+v​b−,v≤0.\displaystyle f(v)=a^{-}+vb^{-},\ v\leq 0\ .

One obtains

ρϵ−=a−−12b−,ρϵ+=a++12​b+,qϵ−=−12a−+13b−,qϵ+=12​a++13​b+\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \rho_{\epsilon}^{-}&=a^{-}-\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}b^{-}\ ,\quad&\rho_{\epsilon}^{+}&=a^{+}+\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}b^{+}\ ,\\[8.5359pt] q_{\epsilon}^{-}&=-\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}a^{-}+\displaystyle\frac{1}{3}b^{-}\ ,\quad&q_{\epsilon}^{+}&=\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}a^{+}+\displaystyle\frac{1}{3}b^{+}\ \end{aligned}

and

∫01v2​f​(v)​𝑑v=−16​ρϵ++qϵ+,\displaystyle\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}v^{2}f(v)dv=-\displaystyle\frac{1}{6}\rho_{\epsilon}^{+}+q_{\epsilon}^{+}\ , ∫−10v2​f​(v)​𝑑v=−16​ρϵ−−qϵ−.\displaystyle\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{0}v^{2}f(v)dv=-\displaystyle\frac{1}{6}\rho_{\epsilon}^{-}-q_{\epsilon}^{-}\ .

Finally, integrating the kinetic equation with respect to the corresponding half-spaces, we get the half-moment approximation of the kinetic equation as

{∂tρϵ++∂xqϵ+=−1ϵ​(ρϵ+−(ρϵ2+3​qϵ4))∂tqϵ++∂x(−16​ρϵ++qϵ+)=−1ϵ​(qϵ+−(ρϵ4+qϵ2))∂tρϵ−+∂xqϵ−=−1ϵ​(ρϵ−−(ρϵ2−3​qϵ4))∂tqϵ−+∂x(−16​ρϵ−−qϵ−)=−1ϵ​(qϵ−−(−ρϵ4+qϵ2)).\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcl}\partial_{t}\rho_{\epsilon}^{+}+\partial_{x}q_{\epsilon}^{+}&=&-\displaystyle\frac{1}{\epsilon}\left(\rho_{\epsilon}^{+}-\left(\displaystyle\frac{\rho_{\epsilon}}{2}+\frac{3q_{\epsilon}}{4}\right)\right)\\[8.5359pt] \partial_{t}q_{\epsilon}^{+}+\partial_{x}\left(-\displaystyle\frac{1}{6}\rho_{\epsilon}^{+}+q_{\epsilon}^{+}\right)&=&-\displaystyle\frac{1}{\epsilon}\left(q_{\epsilon}^{+}-\left(\displaystyle\frac{\rho_{\epsilon}}{4}+\frac{q_{\epsilon}}{2}\right)\right)\\[8.5359pt] \partial_{t}\rho_{\epsilon}^{-}+\partial_{x}q_{\epsilon}^{-}&=&-\displaystyle\frac{1}{\epsilon}\left(\rho_{\epsilon}^{-}-\left(\displaystyle\frac{\rho_{\epsilon}}{2}-\frac{3q_{\epsilon}}{4}\right)\right)\\[8.5359pt] \partial_{t}q_{\epsilon}^{-}+\partial_{x}\left(-\displaystyle\frac{1}{6}\rho_{\epsilon}^{-}-q_{\epsilon}^{-}\right)&=&-\displaystyle\frac{1}{\epsilon}\left(q_{\epsilon}^{-}-\left(-\displaystyle\frac{\rho_{\epsilon}}{4}+\frac{q_{\epsilon}}{2}\right)\right).\\ \end{array}\right. (28)

Introducing the even-odd variables

5.1.3 The extrapolation length

To estimate the accuracy of our method, we consider the classical problem of determining the so-called extrapolation length [33, 37, 25].

For x∈ℝ+,v∈[−1,1]x\in\mathbb{R}^{+},v\in[-1,1] we consider the half space equation

v​∂xf=−(f−(ρ2+32​v​q))\displaystyle v\partial_{x}f=-\left(f-(\frac{\rho}{2}+\frac{3}{2}vq)\right)

with ∫−11v​f​𝑑v=q=0\int_{-1}^{1}vfdv=q=0 and f⁡(0,v)=v,v>0f(0,v)=v,v>0. That means, we consider

v​∂xf=−(f−ρ2).\displaystyle v\partial_{x}f=-\left(f-\frac{\rho}{2}\right)\ .

The extrapolation length is the value of λ∞=f⁡(∞,v)=ρ∞2\lambda_{\infty}=f(\infty,v)=\frac{\rho_{\infty}}{2}. The Maxwell approximation gives λ∞=23\lambda_{\infty}=\frac{2}{3}. The above half moment approximation gives

ρ∞4+a4​γ=q+​(0)=13\displaystyle\frac{\rho_{\infty}}{4}+\frac{a}{4}\gamma=q_{+}(0)=\frac{1}{3}
ρ∞2+(3​a+12)​γ=ρ+​(0)=12.\displaystyle\frac{\rho_{\infty}}{2}+(\frac{3a+1}{2})\gamma=\rho_{+}(0)=\frac{1}{2}.

This leads to

ρ∞=9​a+46​a+3\displaystyle\rho_{\infty}=\frac{9a+4}{6a+3}

and with a2=13a^{2}=\frac{1}{3} we obtain

ρ∞=3​3+42​3+3.\displaystyle\rho_{\infty}=\frac{3\sqrt{3}+4}{2\sqrt{3}+3}.

Thus, the extrapolation length is approximated as λ∞∼0.7113\lambda_{\infty}\sim 0.7113. The exact value computed from a spectral method is 0.71040.7104, see [16, 32]. This yields an error for the above half-moment method of approximately 0.1%0.1\%. In contrast, the Maxwell approximation gives 0.66660.6666, which is an error of 6.1%6.1\%. The variational method in [33, 25] gives 0.70830.7083, which is an error of 0.3%0.3\%.

In this subsection we determine the coupling conditions on the basis of the half-moment approximation of the half-space problem. Multiplying with vv and integrating the kinetic coupling conditions (6) with respect to the positive and negative half moments gives

For a uniform node with equal distribution ci​j=1n−1,i≠jc_{ij}=\frac{1}{n-1},i\neq j and 00 otherwise, one obtains using the equality of fluxes

n−22​n​q∞i+ρ∞i4+a4​γi=n−22​n​q∞j+ρ∞j4+a4​γj.\displaystyle\frac{n-2}{2n}q^{i}_{\infty}+\frac{\rho^{i}_{\infty}}{4}+\frac{a}{4}\gamma^{i}=\frac{n-2}{2n}q^{j}_{\infty}+\frac{\rho^{j}_{\infty}}{4}+\frac{a}{4}\gamma^{j}.

or the invariance of

With the half moment approximations (32) this reads

3​q∞i4+ρ∞i2+(3​a+12)​γi=∑j=1nci​j​(−3​q∞j4+12​ρ∞j+(3​a−12)​γj).\displaystyle\frac{3q^{i}_{\infty}}{4}+\frac{\rho^{i}_{\infty}}{2}+\left(\frac{3a+1}{2}\right)\gamma^{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{ij}\left(-\frac{3q^{j}_{\infty}}{4}+\frac{1}{2}\rho^{j}_{\infty}+\left(\frac{3a-1}{2}\right)\gamma^{j}\right)\ .

Alltogether this yields 2​n2n conditions at a node, i.e. (34), (35), (36) and (37). In combination with the conditions at infinity we have 3​n3n conditions for 3​n3n quantities γi,ρ∞i,q∞i\gamma^{i},\rho^{i}_{\infty},q^{i}_{\infty}.

Note that the invariants (37) and (35) can be combined such that γ\gamma is eliminated, which gives the invariance of

ρ∞+(n−2n)​9​a+4​(n−2n)4​a+2​(n−2n)​q∞.\displaystyle\rho_{\infty}+\left(\frac{n-2}{n}\right)\frac{9a+4\left(\frac{n-2}{n}\right)}{4a+2\left(\frac{n-2}{n}\right)}\ q_{\infty}\ . (38)

All the coupling conditions for the wave equation with uniform nodes derived up to now are given by the conservation of mass (22) and an invariant of the form

ρ+C​q.\displaystyle\rho+Cq\ .

They differ in the factor CC, see Table 1.

With a=13a=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} and n=3n=3 the half moment approximation gives C=0.7313C=0.7313 compared to 0.66660.6666 for Maxwell (24) or 0.50.5 for the full moment approximation. A numerical comparison of the resulting network solutions is presented in the next section.

Remark 5.

For the solution of the wave equation (2), we consider the mathematical entropy

e=12​(ρ2+1a2​q2).\displaystyle e=\frac{1}{2}\left(\rho^{2}+\frac{1}{a^{2}}q^{2}\right).

It evolves according to the conservation law

∂te+∂x(ρ​q)=0.\displaystyle\partial_{t}e+\partial_{x}\left(\rho q\right)=0\ .

Along one edge this entropy is conserved, but the total entropy in the network can change according to the entropy-fluxes at the nodes. Note that for all above models with ρ+C​q=C~\rho+Cq=\tilde{C} and C>0C>0 the total entropy decays, since

∑i=1nρq=∑i=1n(C~−Cq)q=C~∑i=1nq−C∑i=1nq2=−C∑i=1nq2<0.\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\rho\,q=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\tilde{C}-Cq\right)\,q=\tilde{C}\sum_{i=1}^{n}q-C\sum_{i=1}^{n}q^{2}=-C\sum_{i=1}^{n}q^{2}<0\ .

In the following we discuss also the case of an underlying kinetic model with unbounded velocities.

q^=−γ​exp⁡(λ​x)+γ^​exp⁡(−λ​x)+2​a2​π​ρ∞.\displaystyle\hat{q}=-\gamma\exp(\lambda x)+\hat{\gamma}\exp(-\lambda x)+\frac{2a}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\rho_{\infty}.

Since we are only interested in bounded solutions, we have γ^=0\hat{\gamma}=0 and thus

ρ^=γ​λ​exp⁡(λ​x)+22​π​a​q∞q^=−γ​exp⁡(λ​x)+2​a2​π​ρ∞.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \hat{\rho}=\gamma\lambda\exp(\lambda x)+\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}a}q_{\infty}\\ \hat{q}=-\gamma\exp(\lambda x)+\frac{2a}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\rho_{\infty}.\end{aligned} (40)

As before, there are three parameters which can be determined with the three conditions

12​(ρ⁡(0)+ρ^​(0))=ρ+​(0)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left(\rho(0)+\hat{\rho}(0)\right)=\rho_{+}(0)
12​(q⁡(0)+q^​(0))=q+​(0)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left(q(0)+\hat{q}(0)\right)=q_{+}(0)
q∞−a​ρ∞=r1​(0).\displaystyle q_{\infty}-a\rho_{\infty}=r_{1}(0)\ .

Inserting the expressions (40) yields

12​(ρ∞+(λ+2​πa⁡(π−4))​γ+22​π​a​q∞)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left(\rho_{\infty}+\left(\lambda+\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{a(\pi-4)}\right)\gamma+\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}a}q_{\infty}\right) =ρ+​(0)\displaystyle=\rho_{+}(0)
12​(q∞−γ+2​a2​π​ρ∞)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left(q_{\infty}-\gamma+\frac{2a}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\rho_{\infty}\right) =q+​(0)\displaystyle=q_{+}(0)

and for the outgoing quantities ρ−​(0)\rho_{-}(0) and q−​(0)q_{-}(0) we obtain

12​(ρ∞+(−λ+2​πa⁡(π−4))​γ−22​π​a​q∞)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left(\rho_{\infty}+\left(-\lambda+\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{a(\pi-4)}\right)\gamma-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}a}q_{\infty}\right) =ρ−​(0)\displaystyle=\rho_{-}(0)

The Maxwell approximation is in this case given by the equation

q+​(0)=q+​(∞)=12​(q∞+q^∞)=q∞2+a2​π​ρ∞.\displaystyle q_{+}(0)=q_{+}(\infty)=\frac{1}{2}(q_{\infty}+\hat{q}_{\infty})=\frac{q_{\infty}}{2}+\frac{a}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\rho_{\infty}\ .

5.2.3 The extrapolation length

In order to estimate the quality of the above approximation, we consider

v​∂xf=−(f−(ρ+va2​q)​M​(v))\displaystyle v\partial_{x}f=-\left(f-\left(\rho+\frac{v}{a^{2}}q\right)M(v)\right)

with q=0q=0 and k⁡(v)=v​Mk(v)=vM, in order to determine f⁡(∞,v)=λ∞​Mf(\infty,v)=\lambda_{\infty}M. The Maxwell approximation gives ρ∞=2​π2​a\rho_{\infty}=\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{2a}. With the half moment method we obtain

12​(ρ∞+(λ+2​πa⁡(π−4))​γ+22​π​a​q∞)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left(\rho_{\infty}+\left(\lambda+\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{a(\pi-4)}\right)\gamma+\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}a}q_{\infty}\right) =ρ+​(0)=12​π\displaystyle=\rho_{+}(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
12​(q∞−γ+2​a2​π​ρ∞)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left(q_{\infty}-\gamma+\frac{2a}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\rho_{\infty}\right) =q+​(0)=12.\displaystyle=q_{+}(0)=\frac{1}{2}\ .

ρ∞\displaystyle\rho_{\infty} =π​2​π+2​π​(1+a)−2​2​π−8​aa⁡(2​π​π+2​π−2​2​π−4)\displaystyle=\frac{\pi\sqrt{2\pi}+2\pi(1+a)-2\sqrt{2\pi}-8a}{a(\sqrt{2\pi}\pi+2\pi-2\sqrt{2\pi}-4)}

For a=1a=1 this gives ρ∞=1.443\rho_{\infty}=1.443. Compared to the very accurate value 1.43711.4371 obtained with a spectral method [16] this yields an error of 0.4%0.4\%. Maxwell gives 1.25331.2533, which is an error of 12.8%12.8\%. The variational method [34, 25] gives 1.42451.4245 or an error of 0.9%0.9\%.

5.2.4 Coupling conditions

A half space half integration of the coupling conditions gives

q+i​(0)\displaystyle q^{i}_{+}(0) =−∑j=1nci​jq−j(0)\displaystyle=-\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{ij}q_{-}^{j}(0)

which yields

q∞i−γi+2​a2​π​ρ∞i\displaystyle q^{i}_{\infty}-\gamma^{i}+\frac{2a}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\rho^{i}_{\infty} =−∑j=1nci​j(q∞j+γj−2​a2​πρ∞j)\displaystyle=-\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{ij}\left(q^{j}_{\infty}+\gamma^{j}-\frac{2a}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\rho^{j}_{\infty}\right)

Summing these equations gives ∑iq∞i=0\sum_{i}q^{i}_{\infty}=0. Further, for a uniform node we observe the invariance of

n−2n​q∞i−γi+2​a2​π​ρ∞i\displaystyle\frac{n-2}{n}q^{i}_{\infty}-\gamma^{i}+\frac{2a}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\rho^{i}_{\infty} =n−2n​q∞j−γj+2​a2​π​ρ∞j.\displaystyle=\frac{n-2}{n}q^{j}_{\infty}-\gamma^{j}+\frac{2a}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\rho^{j}_{\infty}\ . (41)

Moreover, from

ρ+i​(0)=∑j=1nci​j​ρ−j​(0)\displaystyle\rho^{i}_{+}(0)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{ij}\rho_{-}^{j}(0)

one obtains

ρ∞i+(λ+2​πa⁡(π−4))​γi+2​q∞i2​π​a=∑j=1nci​j​(ρ∞j+(−λ+2​πa⁡(π−4))​γj−2​q∞j2​π​a).\displaystyle\rho^{i}_{\infty}+\left(\lambda+\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{a(\pi-4)}\right)\gamma^{i}+\frac{2\ q^{i}_{\infty}}{\sqrt{2\pi}a}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{ij}\left(\rho^{j}_{\infty}+\left(-\lambda+\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{a(\pi-4)}\right)\gamma^{j}-\frac{2\ q^{j}_{\infty}}{\sqrt{2\pi}a}\right)\,.

Summing these equations we obtain again ∑i=1nγi=0\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma^{i}=0. In the case of a uniform node we can further rearrange, such that

ρ∞i+(n−2n+2​ππ−2)λ​γi+22​π​a​n−2n​q∞i=ρ∞j+(n−2n+2​ππ−2)​λ​γj+22​π​a​n−2n​q∞j\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \rho^{i}_{\infty}+\left(\frac{n-2}{n}+\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{\pi-2}\right)&\lambda\gamma^{i}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}a}\frac{n-2}{n}q^{i}_{\infty}\\ &=\rho^{j}_{\infty}+\left(\frac{n-2}{n}+\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{\pi-2}\right)\lambda\gamma^{j}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}a}\frac{n-2}{n}q^{j}_{\infty}\end{aligned} (42)

holds. Together with the conditions at infinity we have again 3​n3n conditions for 3​n3n quantities γi,ρ∞i,q∞i\gamma^{i},\rho^{i}_{\infty},q^{i}_{\infty}. Combining (41) and (42) we can eliminate the γi\gamma^{i} and obtain as invariant

ρ+n−2n​n−2n​(π−2)​2​π+4​π−82​π​(π−4)+n−2n​(2​π−4)+2​2​π​1a​q.\displaystyle\rho+\frac{n-2}{n}\,\frac{\frac{n-2}{n}(\pi-2)\sqrt{2\pi}+4\pi-8}{\sqrt{2\pi}(\pi-4)+\frac{n-2}{n}(2\pi-4)+2\sqrt{2\pi}}\,\frac{1}{a}\,q\ .

or

ρ+n−2n​1a​4+n−2n​2​π2​π+2​n−2n​q\displaystyle\rho+\frac{n-2}{n}\frac{1}{a}\,\frac{4+\frac{n-2}{n}\sqrt{2\pi}}{\sqrt{2\pi}+2\frac{n-2}{n}}q (43)

The values of the factor CC for the coupling invariants ρ+C​q\rho+Cq for the present case with unbounded velocities are summarized in Table 2.

For a=1a=1 and n=3n=3 this factor is approximately 0.50790.5079. In contrast, the Maxwell approximation gives 0.41780.4178. For a2=13a^{2}=\frac{1}{3} the factor is 6​π6∼0.723\frac{6\pi}{6}\sim 0.723 for Maxwell and approximately 0.87970.8797 for the above half moment formula. This has to be compared to the case of bounded velocities discussed in the last section, where the factor has been determined as 0.73130.7313 for the half-moment- and 0.66660.6666 for the Maxwell approximation. Thus, depending on the underlying kinetic model different coupling conditions are obtained for the same macroscopic equation.

6 Numerical results

In this section we compare the numerical results of the different models on networks. The solutions of the kinetic equation (4) are compared with the half-moment approximation (28) and the macroscopic wave equation (2) with different coupling conditions (24) (25) (38) .

The networks are composed of coupled edges, each arc is given by an interval x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1], which is discretized with 400400 spatial cells if not otherwise stated. In the kinetic model the velocity domain [−1,1][-1,1] is discretized with 400400 cells and we choose ϵ=0.001\epsilon=0.001 if not otherwise stated.

For the advective part of the equations we use an upwind scheme. The source term in the kinetic and half moment equations is approximated with the implicit Euler method. We note that for the wave equation the upwind scheme yields the exact solution by choosing the CFL number equal to 11.

At the nodes we consider in addition to the coupling conditions discussed above for comparison a coupling based on the assumption of equal density at the node, see [41, 18, 28]

ρi\displaystyle\rho^{i} =ρji≠j,i,j=1,2,3\displaystyle=\rho^{j}\qquad i\neq j,\ i,j=1,2,3
∑i=13qi\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{3}q_{i} =0.\displaystyle=0\ .

In general, at the outer boundaries of the network, boundary conditions have to be imposed. For the kinetic problem the values for the ingoing velocities have to be prescribed as mentioned before. For the half-moment approximation the natural boundary conditions are given by integrating the kinetic conditions and using ρ+\rho_{+} and q+q_{+} at left boundaries and ρ−\rho_{-} and q−q_{-} at right boundaries. For the wave equations with full moment, Maxwell and half-moment conditions we use the corresponding approximations discussed above to provide boundary values for the macroscopic equations.

We note that for the boundary values at the right end of the edges we apply the same procedure as detailed in the previous sections for the left end, reversing the spatial orientation in the half space problem. More precisely, a given kinetic inflow ℓ⁡(v)\ell(v) for v∈[−1,0]v\in[-1,0] at the right boundary leads to the following boundary data. In the kinetic model we directly impose f⁡(x=1,v)=ℓ⁡(v)f(x=1,v)=\ell(v) v∈[−1,0]v\in[-1,0], for the half moment model the quantities ρ−=<ℓ(v)>−\rho^{-}=<\ell(v)>_{-} and q−=<vℓ(v)>−q^{-}=<v\ell(v)>_{-} are fixed. In case of the wave equation, the right going Riemann invariant q+a​ρ=Cq+a\rho=C is given by the inner data. The remaining information is given by the following approximations

wave Maxwell <vℓ(v)>−=−ρ4+12q\displaystyle<v\ell(v)>_{-}=-\frac{\rho}{4}+\frac{1}{2}q
wave half-moment {<ℓ(v)>−=12​ρ−34​q+−3​a−12​γ,<vℓ(v)>−=−14​ρ+12​q+a4​γ\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{rl}<\ell(v)>_{-}&=\frac{1}{2}\rho-\frac{3}{4}q+\frac{-3a-1}{2}\gamma,\\ <v\ell(v)>_{-}&=-\frac{1}{4}\rho+\frac{1}{2}q+\frac{a}{4}\gamma\end{array}\right.
wave full-moment <ℓ(v)>−=12ρ−34q,\displaystyle<\ell(v)>_{-}=\frac{1}{2}\rho-\frac{3}{4}q\ ,

which can be obtained by revisiting section 5.1 with x∈[−∞,0]x\in[-\infty,0]. These are used to prescribe the value of the left going characteristic q−a​ρq-a\rho.

6.1 Tripod network

In a first example, we consider a tripod network with initial conditions f1​(x,v)=12f^{1}(x,v)=\frac{1}{2},f2​(x,v)=13f^{2}(x,v)=\frac{1}{3} and f3​(x,v)=0f^{3}(x,v)=0. The corresponding macroscopic states are (ρ1,q1)=(1,0)(\rho^{1},q^{1})=(1,0), (ρ2,q2)=(23,0)(\rho^{2},q^{2})=(\frac{2}{3},0) and (ρ3,q3)=(0,0)(\rho^{3},q^{3})=(0,0). We use free boundary conditions at the exterior boundaries. The computational time is chosen such that the waves generated at the node do not reach the exterior boundaries.

In Figure 4 we compare the kinetic, the half-moment and the wave equation with coupling conditions given by the Maxwell, the half-moment and the full-moment approach and the assumption of equal density at time T=1T=1.

We observe first, that the half moment model gives a very accurate approximation of the kinetic equation. Considering the wave equation with different coupling conditions one observes that the interior state is very accurately approximated by the half moment coupling conditions. Also the Maxwell approximation provides a good approximation in this case. Note that a boundary layer is appearing at the node in the kinetic model, see Figure 5 for a magnification of the situation on edge 11.

Moreover, we investigate the evolution of the total entropy in the network, i.e.

∑i=1312​∫((ρi)2+1a2​(qi)2)​𝑑x.\sum_{i=1}^{3}\frac{1}{2}\int\left((\rho^{i})^{2}+\frac{1}{a^{2}}(q^{i})^{2}\right)dx.

Initially, the total entropy at t=0t=0 is equal to 0.7222220.722222. In this case we use a very fine grid with 3000030000 spatial cells for all models and 400400 cells in velocity space for the kinetic equation. In Table 3 the value of the total entropy at time T=0.1T=0.1 is shown for the different coupling conditions together with the half moment and the kinetic solution for comparison. One observes the very accurate approximation given by the wave equation with half moment coupling conditions. Note, that even for the equal density a small amount of entropy is lost. This is caused by the numerical diffusion in the very last time step, since we have Δ​t<Δ​xa\Delta t<\frac{\Delta x}{a} to hit the final time.

In Table 4 the value of the total entropy at time T=0.1T=0.1 is shown for kinetic and half moment equations for different spatial discretizations.

Finally, we investigate the kinetic equation for different values of ϵ\epsilon. For ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0 the kinetic and the half moment model are very well approximated by the solution of the wave equation with half moment coupling conditions, see Figure 6 and the corresponding magnification at the node in Figure 7.

6.2 Diamond network

As a second example we consider a more complicated network, see Figure 8, as, for example, studied in [20] for the wave equation.

As initial conditions for the kinetic equation we choose f1​(x,v)=1f^{1}(x,v)=1,f2​(x,v)=56f^{2}(x,v)=\frac{5}{6} and fj​(x,v)=12f^{j}(x,v)=\frac{1}{2} for j=3,…,7j=3,\dots,7, which corresponds to macroscopic densities ρ1=2\rho^{1}=2, ρ2=53\rho^{2}=\frac{5}{3} and ρj=1\rho^{j}=1 for j=3,…,7j=3,\dots,7 and fluxes qj=0q^{j}=0 j=1,…,7j=1,\dots,7. These data are also prescribed at the two outer boundaries, i.e. k1​(v)=1k^{1}(v)=1, v∈[0,1]v\in[0,1] and ℓ7​(v)=12\ell^{7}(v)=\frac{1}{2}, v∈[−1,0]v\in[-1,0]. Boundary conditions for the wave equation with full moment, Maxwell and half moment conditions are derived as detailed above. In case of the equal density conditions, we determine the ingoing characteristic using ρ=1,q=0\rho=1,q=0 at the E1E_{1}-boundary and ρ=12,q=0\rho=\frac{1}{2},q=0 at the E7E_{7}-boundary.

In Figure 9 the density ρ4\rho^{4} on edge 44 is displayed at time t=3t=3 and t=10t=10. As before, we observe a good agreement of the half moment coupling with the kinetic and half moment model. Also the Maxwell approximation is relatively close to the kinetic results.

The states of the full moment coupling and the equal density coupling deviate remarkably from the kinetic results. In Figure 10 on the left, ρ4\rho^{4} at time t=50t=50 is shown. All models have reached a stationary state except the equal density coupling. Since the entropy is conserved, a set of waves remains trapped in the network, oscillating back and forth. The stationary states of the models with entropy losses almost coincide.

On the right hand side of Figure 10 the evolution of the total entropy over time is plotted. The total entropy is increasing due to inflow from the boundaries. All models saturate at a certain level, but we again observe a deviation of the equal density and the full moment coupling compared to the accurate Maxwell coupling. In this situation the results for the half-moment coupling, the half moment model and the kinetic model coincide.

7 Conclusion and Outlook

In this work we have derived coupling conditions for the wave equation on a network based on coupling conditions for an underlying kinetic BGK type model via a layer analysis of the situation near the nodes. The presentation in this work includes a new half-moment approximation of the kinetic half-space problem. The general approach can be extended to more complicated problems like linearized Euler equations or kinetic based coupling conditions for nonlinear problems like Burgers and Lighthill-Whitham type equations which will be considered in a forthcoming publication.
